title: How Do Computers Remember?
beats: Recaps last episode (binary, adders) and states today's question: how does a computer remember numbers
Real breadboard circuit: touch a wire, light turns on and stays on after the wire is removed; second wire turns it off
Builds the OR/AND/NOT loop in the simulator; feedback wire from output back into OR is the 'fancy part'; set, release, reset, release
Names it SR latch only after behaviour is seen; introduces NOR as a new building block and packages it as a chip
Second latch from two cross-coupled NOR gates; narrates signals one wire at a time for set and for reset; 'locking' metaphor
Admits this simple-looking setup takes a while to wrap your head around
Adds two AND gates so SET/RESET become DATA+STORE; tests 1 with store off, store on, store off, then 0; renames it data latch
Power-on case: simulation oscillates forever; presenter was confused why real life does not; explains gate delay vs wire speed and random start state
Replicates on real breadboard with NAND chips, 'just to be completely convinced'; shows chip internals, power and ground; tests set/clear; peeks at start state again
Four latches make a 4-bit register sharing one STORE wire
Wires two registers into the ALU, feeds the result back to A; store races around and overwrites 3+1, 4+1, 5+1 uncontrollably
Clock introduced as the fix; flat parts do nothing, rising edge is the only moment to store; motivated by the preceding failure
Edge-triggered flip flop from two latches, first open when clock low, second open when high; tested by changing data in each phase
Tries AND on the clock to gate store; demonstrates the glitch where store toggling fakes a rising edge; says it makes him uneasy
Multiplexer fix: when store is off, feed the stored value back in; builds mux from NOT, 2 AND, OR; tests both store states
Calls it 1-bit register, builds improved 4-bit register, replays the earlier runaway setup: 5+3 lands once as 8 and stays
Wraps up building blocks, teases RAM next episode

metrics.brute_force: yes 5:46: gates are wired and run in the simulator and the dumb version (unclocked store) is built first so its failure motivates the clock
metrics.examples: ~6 circuits in a chain, each fixing the previous one's flaw (SR latch, NOR latch, data latch, flip flop, gated flip flop, mux register); test pattern repeats on every circuit
metrics.ending: Rebuilds the runaway ALU setup with clocked registers and shows it now works, then teases RAM

principles.1: confirmed: opens with a physical light and wire before any gates (0:35)
principles.2: confirmed: names (SR latch, NOR, data latch, flip flop, register) arrive only after behaviour is shown (2:29, 5:46, 14:02)
principles.3: partly: simulator and test rhythm (toggle input, observe output) reused all video, so it becomes habit, but not explicitly taught
principles.4: partly: 'locking the output' (3:44) and the clock as coordinator are loose metaphors, never a sustained analogy
principles.5: confirmed: signal followed wire by wire through each gate (1:40, 3:24, 4:00)
principles.6: confirmed: unclocked store and AND-on-clock tried first, failure shown (10:57, 14:51) before the proper fix
principles.7: confirmed: set/release/reset/release repeated, and the runaway overwrite at 11:13 lets the viewer feel the need for a clock
principles.8: partly: speech steady, but idea rate slows at hard bits through step-by-step tests and repeated retests (13:28-14:02); new nouns spaced roughly every 1-2 min
principles.9: confirmed: every new circuit is tested with the same input sequence
principles.10: confirmed: one bit, then 4 bits, then the ALU loop
principles.11: confirmed: SR latch, data latch, flip flop, register, then RAM teaser; NOR invented as stepping stone (2:29)
principles.12: confirmed: links to previous episode ALU, a diagram found online, real NAND chips, and gate delay physics
principles.13: partly: plain language and honest uncertainty ('I think I roughly understand'); depth via gate delay; tools justified by failures

new_moves.name: fix-the-last-failure
new_moves.what: each new component is introduced only as a repair for a bug demonstrated one beat earlier
new_moves.evidence: 11:13 runaway overwrite leads to clock; 15:09 glitch leads to mux

new_moves.name: reality-check-on-hardware
new_moves.what: rebuilds the abstract simulation on physical breadboard to prove it is not a simulation artifact

theory: Each component enters as the smallest repair for a failure the viewer has just watched, so the vocabulary (latch, clock, edge, mux) is always felt as necessary before it is named. Testing every circuit with the same input choreography turns correctness into something visible instead of asserted.
velocity: Scene builder: support a build-break-fix chain where the broken version is a first-class scene that runs before the fix
Orchestrator: gate any new term behind a shown behaviour; name after demo
Ghost hands: replay the same canonical input sequence on every variant so the learner pattern-matches outputs
Evals: check that every new component is preceded by a demonstrated failure it fixes
Voice: admit confusion honestly at hard steps (4:19) rather than speeding up
